conclusions: The infimum in the extended nonnegative reals of all finite positive t for which the identity function on the symmetric two-point measure at -1 and 1 is measurable, the function x ↦ exp(x^2/(t.toReal)^2) is integrable, and its integral is at most 2, equals the ENNReal embedding of 1/sqrt(log 2).
mathematical_definitions: Let μ = (1/2)δ_{-1} + (1/2)δ_1 on the Borel real line.
Let X : Real → Real be the identity function X(x) = x.
For t in ENNReal, define A(t) to mean that X is measurable, t ≠ 0, t ≠ infinity, x ↦ exp(X(x)^2/(t.toReal)^2) is μ-integrable, and ∫ exp(X(x)^2/(t.toReal)^2) dμ(x) ≤ 2.
The left-hand side is inf {t in ENNReal | A(t)}.
For finite positive t in this concrete setting, the integral equals exp(1/(t.toReal)^2), because X is ±1 with equal mass.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For the real identity function under the measure assigning probability one half to each of -1 and 1, the infimum of all nonzero finite extended-nonnegative scales t such that exp(X^2/(t.toReal)^2) is integrable and has expectation at most 2 is exactly 1 divided by the square root of the natural logarithm of 2, embedded into the extended nonnegative reals.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The proposition is closed: it has no quantified variables and no hypotheses.
Only one concrete measure and one concrete function are covered; no general class of measures, random variables, or functions is quantified over.
Admissible t are explicitly required to be neither zero nor infinity, although the infimum itself need not generally be an admissible member of the set.
ENNReal.toReal sends infinity to zero, but the explicit exclusion t ≠ infinity prevents that totalized behavior from affecting the integrand; t = 0 is also explicitly excluded.
ENNReal.ofReal truncates negative reals to zero, but log 2 is positive, so the asserted right-hand side is the ordinary positive value 1/sqrt(log 2).

The infimum operation is total even for an empty admissible set; in ENNReal the empty-set infimum would be infinity. The asserted finite equality therefore entails that this concrete admissible set is nonempty.

The real integral is a totalized library operation, but admissibility separately requires integrability, so nonintegrable functions cannot qualify merely through the value assigned by the totalized integral.
Measurability and integrability are explicit conjuncts of admissibility rather than consequences encoded by a broader probabilistic abstraction.
